client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. Every time there's a family get-together, I just can't seem to enjoy it the way I used to — her absence is so overwhelming that it kind of overshadows everything else. I'm not even sure talking about it will change how I feel, but I figured I'd give this a try.
therapist: Thank you for being here and giving this a try — that takes courage, especially when you're carrying something this heavy. I can hear in both your words and your voice a deep sadness mixed with a kind of emotional exhaustion, like you're going through the motions of family life while quietly grieving the person who made those moments feel whole. What you're experiencing — that sense of her absence overshadowing joy — is a very real and valid part of grief, and we can gently explore together what thoughts and feelings come up in those moments, without any pressure to "fix" how you feel right away.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, you described it pretty well — it's like I'm physically present at these gatherings but emotionally I'm somewhere else, just waiting for her to walk through the door. Last Sunday we had a birthday dinner for my cousin and I kept looking at her usual chair, and I just felt this hollow, sinking feeling the whole time. I don't know if "exploring" the feelings will help, because honestly I've been trying to avoid them — it just hurts too much to go there.
therapist: That image of you looking at her empty chair says so much — there's a quiet, aching kind of pain in what you're describing, and I notice even in the way you're speaking, there's a softness that feels like you're holding something very tender and fragile right now. Your instinct to avoid the pain makes complete sense — it's one of the most natural responses to grief — but in CBT we often find that avoidance, while protective in the short term, can actually keep us stuck in that hollow feeling rather than moving gently through it. We don't have to dive in all at once; we can take this at whatever pace feels manageable for you.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying about avoidance keeping me stuck, but I'm not sure I fully buy it — like, isn't there something to be said for just giving yourself time to grieve without poking at it constantly? I guess what scares me is that if I actually let myself feel it fully, I won't be able to function, especially at these family events where everyone else seems to be coping better than me. It already feels like I'm barely holding it together as it is.
therapist: You're raising a really valid point — giving yourself time to grieve *is* important, and I want to be clear that I'm not suggesting you force yourself to feel everything at once. What strikes me, though, is that there's a thought underneath what you're saying that might be worth gently examining: the belief that if you let yourself feel this fully, you'll fall apart — and I'm also noticing that comparing yourself to how others seem to be coping might be adding an extra layer of pressure on top of an already heavy load. Grief is rarely as visible in others as it is in ourselves, and "barely holding it together" while showing up to these gatherings actually takes more strength than it might feel like right now.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess I never thought about it that way — that showing up at all is actually something. But when you mention the comparison thing, I think you're right that I do that a lot, like my aunt was laughing and telling stories about my grandmother and I just felt almost angry at her for being able to do that, and then guilty for feeling angry. It's like I'm judging myself for not grieving the "right" way, whatever that even means.
therapist: That layered experience — anger, then guilt, then self-judgment — is so common in grief, yet so exhausting to carry, and I can hear in your voice a kind of quiet distress underneath the words, like you're being hard on yourself even as you're speaking. The truth is, there is no "right" way to grieve — your aunt's laughter and your silent ache at that chair are both valid expressions of love for the same person. What might be worth exploring is that the anger you felt wasn't really about your aunt at all — it may have been grief itself, longing for the ease she seemed to have, and that's something we can be much gentler with yourself about.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: That reframe actually makes some sense to me — that the anger was more about longing than about my aunt specifically. But being "gentler with myself" is one of those things that sounds simple but I genuinely don't know how to do it, like what does that even look like in practice when you're sitting at a dinner table feeling like you're about to cry? It feels like a nice idea that doesn't quite translate into real life for me.
therapist: You're absolutely right to push back on that — "be gentler with yourself" can sound hollow without something concrete to hold onto, and I want to give you something real. In that moment at the dinner table when tears feel close, one small, practical act of self-compassion might look like quietly saying to yourself, "I miss her, and that's okay" — just acknowledging what's true without adding the layer of judgment on top of it. It won't stop the grief, but it interrupts that cycle of feeling bad about feeling bad, which is often what makes those moments feel unbearable rather than just hard.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That's actually a more concrete thing than I expected, and I can see how it might help with the judgment part at least. But I'm a little worried that if I say something like that to myself in the middle of a family dinner, it might actually make me cry more rather than hold it together — and I really don't want to break down in front of everyone and make it about me when it's supposed to be a happy occasion. I guess I'm scared of losing control at the wrong moment.
therapist: I notice there's a kind of urgency in how you're expressing this, like the worry itself is picking up speed — and that fear of losing control in front of others is so understandable, especially when you're already working so hard to hold everything together. It's worth gently questioning the thought underneath that fear though: that crying at a family gathering would mean "making it about you" — because actually, grieving your grandmother *at a family event meant to bring everyone together* is perhaps one of the most natural things in the world, and the people who love you would likely see it as exactly that. And in terms of the practical worry, tears don't always mean losing control — sometimes they're just the body briefly acknowledging what the heart already knows, and they pass.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I think part of me knows you're right that my family would probably understand if I cried, but there's still this voice in my head saying I need to be strong for everyone else, like my mom is grieving too and I don't want to add to her burden. And honestly, the idea that tears "just pass" sounds reassuring in theory, but in the moment it doesn't feel that way — it feels like once I start I won't be able to stop. I guess I'm not fully convinced my own family would know how to handle it if I actually broke down.
therapist: I notice you're speaking quite quickly right now, like part of you is racing to stay ahead of something — and that "I need to be strong for everyone else" voice is one worth pausing on, because it's carrying a lot of weight. There's something worth examining there: you're so focused on protecting your mom from your grief, but is it possible that sharing it together might actually bring you closer rather than burden her — that she might even feel *less* alone knowing you're both missing the same person? The fear that tears won't stop once they start is very common, but it's also a thought, not a fact — and we could gently work on building enough trust in yourself to know that even if it's messy, you would come through it.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: The idea that my mom might actually feel less alone if I opened up to her — I hadn't really considered it from that angle, and it does make me pause. But we've never really been the type of family that talks openly about emotions, so even if the theory is right, I honestly wouldn't know how to start that conversation without it feeling forced or awkward. It's like I can see the door you're pointing to, but I have no idea how to actually open it.
therapist: There's something quietly hopeful in what you just said — you can see the door, and that's actually more progress than it might feel like right now, even if your voice carries a kind of nervous energy, like you're standing right at the edge of something unfamiliar. The good news is that with a family that doesn't have a tradition of emotional openness, the conversation doesn't have to start with a grand declaration — sometimes it can be as small as saying to your mom, "I've been having a hard time at family gatherings without her, do you ever feel that way too?" That one gentle question invites her in without forcing anything, and it lets her meet you halfway if she's ready.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That's a much smaller step than I was imagining, and I think I could actually picture myself saying something like that to her. But I guess my worry is — what if she shuts it down, or just changes the subject, or says something like "we just have to stay strong"? I don't know if I could handle feeling rejected on top of everything else I'm already carrying right now.
therapist: I can hear real anxiety in your voice right now — there's an urgency and intensity there that tells me this fear of rejection feels very immediate and raw, not just hypothetical. It's worth noticing the thought underneath it though: that if your mom deflects, it would mean rejection of *you*, when in reality it might just mean she doesn't yet have the tools to go there — that's about her grief and her limits, not a measure of your worth or your relationship. And even if she does change the subject, you would have done something courageous, and that matters regardless of how she responds — we can work on building enough of a foundation in yourself so that her reaction, whatever it is, doesn't have to determine whether you're okay.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: That distinction — that her pulling away would be about her limits, not a rejection of me — is something I intellectually understand, but I'm not sure I'd actually feel it that way in the moment. I think my whole life I've kind of tied my sense of being okay to how the people around me respond, so if she shuts it down, it would probably still hit me pretty hard no matter how much I tell myself it's not about me. I guess that's a bigger pattern than just this one conversation with my mom.
therapist: There's something really significant happening right now — your words are measured and reflective, but your voice is telling a different story, with an urgency and intensity that suggests this realization is landing somewhere deep and important, not just as an idea but as something you're feeling in real time. What you've just named — tying your sense of being okay to how others respond — is indeed a bigger pattern, and it's actually one of the most meaningful things we've touched on today, because it sits underneath the grief, the fear of crying, the worry about your mom, all of it. That kind of insight is genuinely the beginning of something, and it's exactly the type of pattern that CBT can help you work with in a real and lasting way.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech
